outcomes: Verify cached logits against every full prefix
lessons: Reuse the past without changing the model
Match full-prefix logits, layer by layer
Turn logits into a controlled choice

kv-cache.name: KV cache
kv-cache.definition: Stored attention keys and values from earlier sequence positions.
kv-cache.explanation: During autoregressive decoding, earlier hidden states do not change. Their projected keys and values can be retained in each decoder layer and reused by later queries. This avoids repeating their projection and feed-forward work. Cache memory still grows with layers, sequence positions, request batch size, head width, and precision, and every new query still reads the relevant cached keys and values during attention.

top-k-sampling.name: top-k sampling
top-k-sampling.definition: Sampling after retaining only the k highest-logit token IDs.
top-k-sampling.explanation: Top-k sampling ranks candidate token IDs by logit, excludes every token outside the first k, renormalizes the remaining probability mass, and draws one token ID from that smaller set. With k equal to one it becomes greedy decoding. A larger k allows more variety but can admit weak candidates. The useful setting depends on the model, prompt, temperature, evaluation goal, and desired run reproducibility.

continuous-batching.name: continuous batching
continuous-batching.definition: Changing the active request batch between one-token decoding iterations.
continuous-batching.explanation: Autoregressive serving advances requests one token at a time. Continuous batching uses those iteration boundaries to admit new requests and remove finished ones, rather than holding a fixed batch until its longest request completes. Each request retains separate tokens, cache, stopping state, and randomness. Actual gains depend on kernel shapes, scheduling overhead, cache capacity, fairness policy, and the request-length distribution.

token-streaming.name: token streaming
token-streaming.definition: Delivering sampled token IDs before the whole response is complete.
token-streaming.explanation: A streaming interface emits each available token or text chunk as generation proceeds. The user can begin reading after the first token, reducing perceived latency and time to first output. Streaming does not inherently reduce the model computations or total completion time. A deployed stream additionally needs cancellation, backpressure, error signaling, and a transport protocol that preserves chunk order across the complete response.
